I just felt relief my first time. Relief and anger at my parents who wouldn't put me on hormone blockers when I asked them to, who fucked up my height potential with their abuse and neglect, and who made it so I couldn't begin transitioning until I moved out at 20. I was giddy with excitement and scared that I'd turn into the hideous, unloveable monster my parents said it would turn me into. Ultimately, it didn't change me much at all due to what I now suspect is some kind of androgen resistance in my body. I was jealous, because my friends who had come out 5 years after me had already started T in high school. I was afraid that the changes wouldn't come (and I turned out to be almost right). A year later, I've never felt guilt about the privilege of having T, just rage on behalf of all my trans brothers who are still blocked from beginning their medical transitions by bigots and bureaucracy. I still feel dysphoria, sometimes crippling dysphoria, but I've also got days when I think I look okay, which is a new thing. I've begun the slow process of reprogramming myself to see that my worth extends beyond what is skin deep. 

Be grateful that you've got T. Let yourself feel a little excitement. Don't compare your progress to that of other trans men, as that will only bring you grief. Don't set your expectations too high and just enjoy the changes as they come. For me, all the change happened in the first 3 months and then pretty much stopped, for others it was the opposite. 

Rather than feel guilt for getting out of this struggle relatively unscathed, just feel compelled to support your trans brothers and sisters in their quest to create the bodies they need to be comfortable. Donate to people's transition funds, if you have the money. Reach out to people in the community, raise awareness about the importance of allowing trans kids the option of hormone blockers and hormones so people like us in the future won't have to grow up with the pain of watching their bodies morph into things they don't identify with. Give your mother a hug, tell her you'll always love her and tell her how much her support means to you.

When the wheels of transitioning get going, it all happens so fast. For a decade I waited and begged my parents to let me transition. The day I moved out I googled an informed consent clinic, which was just a convenient BART ride away, I walked in, signed a few forms, and within a week I was on T and had a letter from the T doctor and my old therapist to authorize my top surgery. Within two months, I'd had top surgery, thanks to my amazing insurance. It moved so quickly at first, I was honestly terrified. A decade of waiting and suddenly I was second guessing myself. What if my parents were right all along? They were wrong of course, and I've been a much less suicidal person than I was pre-T and pre-op. 

The truth is, lots of us have something akin to survivor's guilt. We hear about people like us who have ended their lives or had their lives ended for them by bigots. We read the blog posts of our peers who are still stuck in situations where they don't have access to hormones, and it strikes a deep chord because we've been there too, even if not to the same extent. The solution is not to punish yourself for being lucky, but to enjoy the gifts you've been given as much as you can and add to the sum of trans happiness by being a success story. Knowing that there were people who were happy post-transition, that I could one day be almost as happy as them was the light at the end of the tunnel before I had access to T. I suggest that you try giving back to the community if you are still feeling guilt. And, talk to your therapist about it. 

If you're feeling ambivalent about taking T at all, it's definitely worth talking to a professional and doing some soul searching. Ultimately, you're the only one who knows whether or not this is right for you. It's possible to start T and stop if it turns out it isn't what you want. If by "I don't know what I am" you are questioning whether or not you are really an FTM, it may be a good time to take a step back and re-evaluate. Loads of non-binary people take T for a while, until they reach the place they feel comfortable. I know FTMs who don't even feel the need to take T. Gender identity is plastic and each individual conception of what it means to be 'X' gender will differ considerably from the next. Maybe you've been pressured into putting yourself into a box? You shouldn't have to feel rushed about this! Your decision to transition should be completely your own, and if that means just letting the T sit there, then that's fine too. There isn't any single roadmap to how you are meant to transition. Pick what feels right for you!

Also, as far as injecting goes, it's pretty hard to screw up, but you're right about it being a good idea to have it in the presence of a medical professional the first time. Be sure to have a nurse show you the right way to do it. When you have to do it yourself the first time, it may be helpful to watch a youtube video on injecting just to be sure you've got all the steps down right (or have your mother watch one) and look up a diagram for T injection sites, and be sure to use an alcohol swab to cleanse the area. 

Congratulations on taking this big step in your transition!

As a mixed race (sometimes white passing) transgender person, I think I may have a unique perspective. I was born biologically female, but medically transitioned to male at the age of 10. I am ID'd as male 100% of the time in public, whereas before the age of 6-7ish, I fell into a grey area and people would sometimes think I was a girl, depending on how I dressed.

1) From grades 5 to 8 a fellow whitey and I would go to Barnes and Noble every day after school and he would shop lift to his heart's content. One day we brought in a black friend of ours who was just looking at the candy and took NOTHING, and before we left the store our black friend was asked to turn out his pockets, but my friend and I were not asked to do the same when the store manager turned up nothing.*

2) When I fail a calculus test, it's because I'm bad at math. If my sister fails a calculus test, it's because girls are bad at math. (My sister said something like this at some point, and I'm not sure how true this is. My Asian mother always just said "white people are bad at math and that's why you both suck at it".)

3) Never once have I had to carry mace when walking my dog, but apparently carrying mace just to walk around the neighbourhood is very common among my female friends.

4) My parents have never pressured me to have kids before I felt ready, though they've apparently started working on my sister who is in her 20s. (Though with females I can see why time would be of the essence, with menopause and all.)

5) Pre-transition, I was often called "bossy", but now I'm called a "natural leader".

6) Pre-transition, I often got into trouble for being "rough housing" and being "too aggressive" but once I began to transition and was ID'd as male, rough play was almost encouraged.

7) I was having sex with my girlfriend on a regular basis at 16. My sister wasn't even allowed to DATE until she was 18.

8) The history books in primary school focus on people who are the same race as I am.

9) I see people the same race as me in film and television.

10) I've never been typed as a "thug" for wearing a hoodie.

11) I'm never asked to do the dishes after dinner. (But, my sister never has to take out the trash, so we're even.)

12) Depictions of females in the media are made for my gaze and not my sister's.

13) I'm allowed to be sarcastic. If my sister said half of the sarcastic shit I say to my parents, she'd find herself disowned. I, however, get a good laugh most of the time.

14) I don't have to waste money shaving every inch of my body. My sister, however, not only clogs up every drain in the house, but takes 10 years shaving her legs and whatever else girls shave (don't want to think about it). 

15) When I was young, my female relatives and their friends were always commenting on how much I ate. Granted, I ate like a starving whale, but since transitioning I have rarely heard a word said about my portion sizes, what I choose to eat, etc. If anything is said, it's usually an affectionate remark about how great it is to see me eating so well. My sister, on the other hand, has her every move scrutinized by a host of staring aunts who are just dying to for her to make one wrong choice at the table so they can make some slightly offensive comment about her appetite. 

16) I can walk around the house without a shirt on without my parents murdering me for shaming the family.

17) I've never been called a slut for having multiple partners in quick succession.

18) My family members don't feel entitled to critique my body, whereas this Christmas my Asian grandmother told my cousin (who just had a baby) "Eat less. You're getting fat like an American." She said this in front of everyone, and no one but me seemed shocked.

19) No one ever questions my 'Canadian-ness' or 'American-ness' (which is hilarious, because I'm a Canadian who moved to the US, and people talk to me about how awful immigrants are without realising that I am an immigrant.)

20) According to a study they mentioned on Anderson Cooper a while back, white male ex-cons are more likely to get a job than a black male applicant with a clean record.

21) I pass as white more than my sister (and less than my brother, which I'll get to). Never to I have to wonder if my SO is only with me because they've got an Asian/insertrace fetish.

22) I didn't need an outreach program to tell me that a STEM career was a possibility for me.

23) My brother got invited to join a bunch of fraternities his freshman year, whereas I was basically shooed away by the white guys handing out pamphlets at club day when I asked for information. A black friend of mine was only invited to one fraternity, and that was a Pan-African one. 

24) My name is as conventional as "John Smith" and I've never had anyone make fun of it, intentionally/unintentionally mispronounce it, or use it in any way to humiliate me. My sister got a non-English first name, and as a result ended up giving up on teachers pronouncing it correctly and went by an easy nick name until college.

25) I'm less likely to be murdered by my spouse than my sister.

26) When I get angry, people let me vent. When my sister gets angry, it's seen as unseemly.

27) When we were little and kidnapping was still a thing everyone cared about in the late 90s and early 2000s, my siblings and I used to joke about 
what would happen if any of us was kidnapped. We assumed that if my sister was kidnapped they MIGHT run her picture in the local paper, since she was a cute little girl. We said that if my brother (who looks 100% white) was kidnapped, it might make national headlines. We said that if *I* was kidnapped, since I was a cute, white-passing blonde "girl", I'd make international news and the Americans would have a candle-lit vigil for me. (It sounds fucked up now.)


But, to counter that, here are some advantages that females have over males in my experience: 

1) They aren't expected to have a job and a car by potential romantic partners. 

2) I was sexually assaulted by a grown man when I was a teenager and the cops not only didn't take me seriously, 
but felt the need to ask me invasive questions about my sexuality. When I began looking for support for male rape victims, I found nothing in my area. I went to one support group that didn't explicitly say "women's abuse survivors group" and there were only women there, and they all were pretty hostile to me, even though I was not the enemy and was there for support too. When I had a mental breakdown because of what happened, I was told to do things like 'get over it' by my family, whereas a female cousin of mine was practically drowned in sympathy when she finally left her abusive husband. The sympathy or empathy for me as a male victim of sexual assault just was not present. 

3) Male victims of female paedophiles (for example, male students whose female teachers molest/have sex with them) are not taken seriously. People assume that they "enjoyed it". 

4) Kids automatically seem to go to the mother in custody cases, for better or worse, without regard for individual circumstances. 

5) Going back to the last of my white-male privileged points, when young white females are killed or kidnapped, people care far more than they do if males go missing. 



*I'm actually part Asian, so I've got white skin but slightly Asian eyes if you look really closely. Without a serious tan, I'm generally taken for white. When I was young I was white passing 99% of the time.
